Zuma Jailed

By: Kate Barry | Paid

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Jacob Zuma sentenced to 15 months imprisonment

Unique Selling Point:
A hugely significant judgment by the Constitutional Court found former President Jacob Zuma guilty of contempt of court, and sentenced him to 15 months direct imprisonment. How did he land up behind bars, and what does this mean for South Africa?

Script:


ZUMA JAILED

Judge: I find myself with no option but to commit Mr Zuma to imprisonment in the hope that doing so sends an unequivocal message: In this, our constitutional dispensation, the rule of law and the administration of justice prevails.

V/O: Today would have been D-Day for former President Jacob Zuma - the deadline for him to kiss his fire-pool goodbye and place himself in custody. But, in a surprise twist yesterday, the Constitutional Court agreed to hear Zuma’s urgent application to have the judgment rescinded. While denying he is guilty of contempt, Zuma insists the Court should reconsider sending him to prison because of his advanced age and medical condition.

Judge: Mr Jacob Gedleyihlekisa Zuma is sentenced to undergo 15-months imprisonment.

Link: When Acting Chief Justice Sisi Kamphephe found Zuma guilty of contempt of court South Africans could hardly believe their ears. It was the Constitutional Court stamping its authority with booming clarity.

Richard: Mr Zuma was the architect of his own misfortune. He backed himself into this legal corner, and I think the Court had really no choice but, first of all, to find him guilty of contempt, and secondly to punish him for it.

V/O: Richard Calland is Professor of Public Law at the University of Cape Town.

Richard: It’s a sad day, but it’s also a day to be very proud, I think Bongani, of South Africa’s democracy. The rule of law has stood firm. If we owe Mr Zuma anything, it is that he’s provided our Constitution and our rule of law and our courts with the opportunity to prove that they are more than just pieces of paper.

V/O: On the day of his inauguration in 2009, the heavens opened. The rain proved to be a blessing for President Zuma and his close associates, but for the nation less so. It’s estimated that the Gupta family stole over R49 billion during his presidency. Initially it was former Public Protector Thuli Madonsela who investigated those allegations.

Thuli: I am convinced now that former President Zuma does not want to answer the questions. We saw that when he gave me and my team the runaround. Promises to give us answers, but as soon as we provided him with a Section 79 notice that indicated he might be more complicated than in the original allegations, it became clear that he didn’t have an appetite to account.

Bongani: Do you sometimes feel that Deputy Chief Justice Raymond Zondo is experiencing the frustration you did?

Thuli: I do think he is experiencing the same frustration in some ways.
And in the end, we couldn’t conclude this investigation.

V/O: The remedial action prescribed in her 2016 State of Capture report was a Commission of Inquiry. From Day 1 President Zuma tried to block this by challenging the validity of Madonsela’s report. He lost the case in every court, including the Constitutional Court.

Link: Despite dragging his feet, it was President Zuma who eventually established the Zondo Commission of Inquiry into State Capture in 2018. But when it came to his turn to provide answers, he didn’t co-operate – not fully. He frustrated any attempts to get straight answers – eventually saying he’d rather go to prison than appear before Judge Zondo. Well, this Court has said so be it.

Judge: Although Mr Zuma is no longer President, his conduct flies in the face of the obligation he bore as President. It is disturbing that he, who twice swore allegiance to the Republic, its laws and the Constitution, has sought to ignore, undermine and in many ways destroy the rule of law altogether.

V/O: Zuma appeared briefly at the Commission in July 2019, but his answers were vague and unhelpful.

Zuma: No I’ve got no idea what’s happening here.

V/O: Claiming he’d been subjected to a rude interrogation, Zuma abandoned his testimony and left the building.

Derek: Let me ask you, will you be back? You will be back.

Zuma: I would be.

Derek: Ok great, see you.

V/O A year later he claimed that Justice Zondo was biased against him and demanded his recusal. When Zondo refused to do so, Zuma walked out of the Commission mid-session in November 2020.

V/O: This prompted the Commission to launch an urgent application to the Constitutional Court to order Zuma to testify. With good reason says Constitutional Law expert Professor Pierre de Vos.

Pierre: One of the reasons I believe the Commission went to the Court directly is because of the long, long history of former President Zuma abusing the court process to try never to have to actually get to the end of any process. To delay…the so-called Stalingrad option.

V/O In January this year the Constitutional Court ordered Zuma to obey the Zondo Commission. When he refused, the Commission asked the Court to find him guilty of contempt. When the Chief Justice then asked Zuma to suggest an appropriate punishment, Zuma responded with an open letter of defiance.

Judge: His conduct demonstrates a deliberate choice to once again air his views though inflammatory statements intended to undermine this Court’s authority and portray himself as a victim of the law.
Judge: Never before has this Court’s authority and legitimacy been subjected to the kinds of attacks that Mr Zuma has elected to launch against it and its members. Never before has the judicial process been so threatened.

Pierre: For me in some way, a contempt of court matter is a more serious abuse of power than the corruption matters than the former president is going to be prosecuted for. Because with the contempt case he deliberately launched a campaign against the judiciary and the Constitutional Court based on complete lies and falsehoods.

V/O: For the hundreds of thousands of South Africans who joined the 2017 Zuma Must Fall marches, this seems like justice at last. But for Zuma supporters, the idea of him behind bars is unthinkable, according to MK Military Veterans spokesperson Carl Niehaus.

Carl: You must understand that there is an upwelling of outrage and anger about this sentence imposed on President Zuma by a very large part of the South African population. The support base of President Zuma in South African society has never been questioned. He is probably still the most popular politician in our country.

Sfx: We are Zuma, Zuma is us!

Bongani: Are you worried that this situation could get out of hand?

Carl: Obviously we are concerned. This judgment is now seen by a very large part of the population of South Africa as the judiciary getting involved in factional politics. We now have a dictatorship of the judiciary, and under those circumstances there is going to be outrage. There is going to be upheaval.

V/O: The Jacob Zuma Foundation has denounced Judge Khampepe’s judgment as judicially emotional & angry and not consistent with our Constitution.”

Thuli: President Zuma might know 100% of what he’s saying is not true. But people who support him genuinely think that he is a good person, will support him blindly and take his word as gospel. And I think that’s how lies are peddled globally. That’s how we’ve become the age of fake news.

Richard: I suspect that support for Mr Zuma is not as significant as he may hope for. Clearly for a number of months now, he’s been trying to stir up political unrest, political foment, trying to create a political crisis around this, given that he’s run out of legal runway. But I think that moment will come and go. And unfortunately for Mr Zuma, he faces the inevitable consequence of his choices, his actions and indeed, his misconduct.

Link: With former President Jacob Zuma behind bars the African National Congress is placed in an interesting position. Will the reality of his imprisonment sow further division in the ruling party, or will it finally bring about the long promised era of accountability?

Richard: I think if anything, it strengthens the reform group’s hand. It strengthens Cyril Ramaphosa because what it does is show that if you are guilty of misconduct, you will face the consequences. I think it helped tilt the balance in favour of accountability as opposed to impunity.

V/O: Like any other prisoner Zuma would be eligible to apply for parole. If he only served a third of his sentence, he could be home by Christmas. But any thoughts of a presidential pardon are unrealistic.

Pierre: Usually these processes take a year, 2 years, 3 years. So a pardon is not practically, really possible unless all the rules are thrown out of the window.

Richard: It would be counter-productive to the reform programme, the rebuilding of public trust in battered pubic institutions. So I think it both unlikely and highly inappropriate. I honestly believe that Mr Zuma is yesterday’s man and that history is moving on.

V/O: The Constitutional Court will hear the urgent application on Monday the 12th of July.
